To annoy someone means to cause them a feeling of mild irritation, impatience, or displeasure. When you annoy someone, you make them feel bothered — not deeply hurt, not furious, but uncomfortable in a nagging, "I wish this would stop" kind of way.

Think of it like a fly buzzing near your ear. It is not dangerous. It does not cause serious pain. But it keeps bothering you, and you cannot ignore it. That is the feeling of being annoyed.
The Emotional Level — How Strong Is It?

This is one of the most important things to understand about "annoy." It describes a mild to moderate level of emotional discomfort. It is not a heavy word.

Picture a scale of emotional disturbance:

Bother → Annoy → Irritate → Upset → Anger → Infuriate

"Annoy" sits on the lighter end of this scale. It does not mean to make someone deeply sad, traumatized, or explosively angry. If a sound annoys you, you feel impatient and wish it would stop. You have not been wounded or destroyed by it.

That said, something that annoys you repeatedly over time can eventually make you genuinely angry. The annoyance builds up. But the act of "annoying" itself points to that mild, persistent discomfort — not the final explosion.

This is wonderfully flexible. Almost anything can be the subject of "annoy":

A person can annoy another person:

My brother annoys me when he talks too loudly on the phone.

A thing (sound, smell, habit) can annoy someone:

The constant dripping of the tap annoys the entire family.

A situation or fact can annoy someone:

It annoys me that the bus is always late.

Notice in that last example the structure: "It annoys me that..." — this is extremely common in English and very natural. You are not annoyed by a person; you are annoyed by a situation or circumstance.

One subtle but crucial point: you can annoy someone completely by accident, without any intention. The word does not require the "annoyer" to be doing it on purpose.

The dog's barking annoys the neighbors. (The dog has no intention — but the effect is real.)

She did not mean to, but her habit of repeating herself annoyed her colleagues.

However, annoy can also describe deliberate behavior:

He knew she was trying to study, but he kept interrupting her just to annoy her.

So the word works in both directions — accidental and deliberate. What matters is the effect on the person being annoyed, not the intention behind it.

Learning the patterns will help you use "annoy" naturally:

1. [Subject] annoys [person]:

Loud music annoys me.

2. [Subject] annoys [person] by [doing something]:

He annoys his roommate by leaving dishes in the sink.

3. It annoys [person] that/when...:

It annoys her when people don't say "thank you."
It annoys me that nobody told me about the meeting.

4. [Person] is annoyed by [something] — passive form:

She was annoyed by the constant interruptions.

5. [Person] finds [something] annoying:

I find his attitude really annoying.
Do you find it annoying when people are late?
Words That Are Similar — And How They Differ

Irritate — Nearly identical to "annoy" in meaning. Slightly more formal. Often used for physical irritation too (a chemical can irritate your skin). When used emotionally, it is interchangeable with "annoy" in most situations, though "irritate" can sometimes imply a slightly sharper or more persistent feeling.

Bother — Slightly softer and more general than "annoy." To bother someone can mean to disturb, trouble, or mildly annoy them. "Sorry to bother you" is much gentler than "Sorry to annoy you."

Bug (informal) — A casual, everyday synonym for annoy.

It really bugs me when people chew loudly.

Pester — A specific type of annoying. To pester means to annoy someone by repeatedly asking for something or following them around.

The children pestered their mother for ice cream all afternoon.

Nag — To annoy someone by repeatedly criticizing them or reminding them to do something.

He nagged her about finishing her homework every single evening.

Vex — A more formal and slightly stronger word than annoy. To vex someone means to cause them irritation and worry. Used more in formal writing or older texts.

Get on someone's nerves — A very common idiom that means the same thing as annoy.

His constant whistling gets on my nerves.
To please, delight, soothe, or comfort someone are the natural opposites — to give them a positive or calming feeling rather than an irritating one.

These are natural combinations you will hear frequently:

  • "It really annoys me that..." — used to express frustration about a situation
  • "Stop annoying me!" — a direct command to someone bothering you
  • "What annoys me is..." — used to explain a specific irritant
  • "I find it annoying when..." — a softer, more reflective way to express the same
  • "Don't annoy the animals" — a common warning in zoos or when near pets
  • "You're being really annoying right now" — using the adjective form to describe someone's current behaviour

"Annoy" almost always needs an object — there must be a person (or group) being annoyed. You annoy someone. You cannot simply say "He annoys" and stop there; it sounds incomplete. The exception is the adjective form: "He is annoying" or "That sound is annoying," which can stand alone.
Putting It All Together — A Mental Picture

Imagine you are trying to sleep. A mosquito keeps flying near your ear. It buzzes. You swat it. It comes back. It buzzes again. You are not devastated. You are not weeping. You are not in a blind rage. But you are bothered. You are impatient. You want it to stop.

That mosquito is annoying you.

Now replace the mosquito with a person tapping their pen in a quiet room, or a car alarm going off outside your window, or a colleague who interrupts you every five minutes — the feeling is the same. Mild, persistent, nagging discomfort that you wish would go away.

That is precisely what "annoy" means.
